title: WPMS/706/2011 of VINOD KUMAR Vs MANAGING DIRECTOR UTTARANCHAL S.R.T.C.and ANOTHER

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT
NAINITAL
Writ Petition No. 706 (M/S) of 2011
Vinod Kumar ....... Petitioner
vs.
Managing Director Uttaranchal S.R.T.C. & Another

...... Respondents
Mrs. Neetu Singh, Advocate for the petitioner.
Mr. Ashish Joshi, Advocate for the respondents.
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J. (Oral)
1. Brief facts of the present case are that the petitioner
was appointed as a Conductor with the U.P. State Road
Transport Corporation, and at the relevant time when the
controversy has arisen i.e. in the year 2001, he was
attached to the Rishikesh Depot as a Conductor. It chanced
so that bus bearing its registration No.U.P.07 L 9366,
which was being plied by the Corporation for a route from
Delhi to Rishikesh and Rishikesh to Srinagar.
2. It is the case of the petitioner before this Court that
since the journey scheduled to be undertaken by the bus
was a long distance journey, hence it was being operated
by two crew members, one crew member was to operate
from Delhi to Rishikesh and second crew member takes
over the remaining part of journey from Rishikesh to
Srinagar. As per the allegation, which finds place in the
charge-sheet issued to the petitioner on 19.11.2001 was
that the inspecting team of the respondent-Corporation, in
the mid night at about 0.03 hours, had stopped the bus at
'Rampur Tiraha' Muzaffar Nagar on 25.10.2001 and it is

-2-
the case of the respondents that during the course of
investigation it was found that bus in total was carrying 39
passengers and according to the respondents out of those
39 passengers, 33 passengers was scheduled to undertake
the journey from Delhi to Srinagar, 5 passengers from
Delhi to Devprayag and 1 passenger from Delhi to
Srinagar.
3. The allegation of respondents is that the petitioner
has committed a misconduct as defined under Rule 61 of
the Rules governing the service conditions of the petitioner
i.e. U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Employees
Service Regulation, 1981, because as per the case in the
chargesheet, the charge was that the petitioner was found
guilty of issuing short distance tickets to the passengers
being carried in the bus on 25.10.2001.
4. The case of the respondents was that the petitioner
after having received the fare from the 33 passengers
travelling from Delhi to Srinagar had issued a short
distance tickets from Delhi to Rishikesh only. Similarly,
he has also issued a short distance tickets to the five
passengers who as a matter of fact were travelling from
Delhi to Devprayag, who too were issued the tickets upto
Rishikesh only. Consequently, they have concluded in the
chargesheet that Corporation had suffered a loss of
Rs.2535/-. To substantiate the spot investigation which
was said to have been conducted by the respondent-Corporation on 25.10.2001, when the bus was stopped,
they contend that the fact of issuing short distance tickets

-3-
revealed from the "statement of the passengers", which
was recorded by them on the spot. The fact of recording of
statement of passengers, the same would find place in the
findings recorded by the inquiry officer dated 22.3.2002.
What is relevant at this stage is that when the statement
was recorded on 15.2.2002 during the course of inquiry
one Mr. Vijay Kumar Singri. i.e. Assistant Transport
Inspector, he was posed with the question, and he answered
that he had taken a written statement of the passengers, but
no date has been mentioned on it. Why? "the answer to the
question", given by the Assistant Transport Inspector was
that he did take the statement of the passengers on the spot,
the fact which could be further verified from the statement
of the passengers itself which was also signed by the
Conductor. For the entire controversy, the supply a copy of
statement of passengers as recorded by Mr. V.K. Singri and
copy of his statement of Mr. V.K. Singri is relevant
because he was the person who was dealing with the fact
pertaining to recording of statement of the passengers and
the mode in which it was recorded.
5. On conclusion of the inquiry and submission of the
report, it was held that the charges as levelled against the
petitioner in the chargesheet are made out and since the
inquiry officer being other than the disciplinary authority,
the matter was referred to the Regional Manager, who was
the appointing authority of the petitioner to take an
appropriate action on basis of the findings of the inquiry
report dated 22.3.2002, as submitted against the petitioner.

-4-
6. On reference of the inquiry report as made to the
Regional Manager, he by the letter no.1101 dated
19.11.2001, a show cause notice was issued to the
petitioner, vide letter no.1470 dated 26.3.2002, wherein he
was called upon to submit his reply, looking to the fact that
the charges against him have been proved to be true, why
not his services may be dismissed?
7. It is the case of the petitioner that after receipt of the
show cause notice dated 26.3.2002, he had submitted his
reply on 8.4.2002 to the Regional Manager, wherein he
denied the finding of the report, and contended in his
defence that looking to the past conduct and also that his
services has been unblemished may also be taken note.
Further more he submitted in reply to the show cause in its
paragraph 4, a specific pleading has been taken that during
the course of investigation, the statement of the passengers
was taken by the Investigating Officer and no credibility
could be attached to those statements for the reason that if
their statements were true, the copy of the same since was
never supplied to petitioner nor he was provided an
opportunity to cross examine those witnesses, so as to
enable the petitioner to extract truth from the passengers by
cross examining them, would vitiate the entire proceedings
for the imposition of proposed major penalty.
8. Learned counsel for the petitioner further submitted
that the entire proceedings were vitiated and the allegations
levelled against him since are not proved beyond doubt for
the reason, it has come in evidence on record, as well as in

-5-
reply to show that it is not the case of the respondents that
tickets were not issued to the passengers and further it is
the case of the petitioner that subsequently after the
inspection conducted on 25.10.2001, the tickets which
were issued to the passengers for the remaining part of
journey the amount was paid by the passengers themselves,
but not by the petitioner.
9. During the course of her arguments, the learned
counsel for the petitioner, Mrs. Neetu Singh, she further
submitted that petitioner's bag was never inspected and
there was no difference in the way bill as compared to the
tickets issued by him, which he was supposed to prepare
while rendering his services as a Conductor. After having
received the reply, the respondents had proceeded to pass
the impugned order on 31.3.2004, whereby, his services
were terminated. It is the case of the petitioner that the
order of termination was passed without providing him
due, adequate and effective opportunity to defend himself
and thereby his services have been wrongly dispensed
with.
10. Being aggrieved against the order dated 31.3.2004,
the petitioner has preferred a departmental appeal on
29.5.2004 as contemplated under the Rule of 1981 and the
said appeal too has been dismissed by the order dated
3.1.2005.
11. On perusal of the appellate court's order, yet again, it
was a reiteration of fact and circumstances which has been
reflected in the order of dismissal dated 31.3.2004, and it

-6-
has been argued by Mrs. Neetu Singh, that as a matter of
fact the appellate court has not exercised its independent
mind to consider the circumstances under which the
inspection was conducted and the report, which is on the
basis of dismissing the services of the petitioner was
prepared and submitted.
12. Aggrieved against the order of dismissal dated
31.3.2004, as well as the appellate order dated 3.1.2005,
the petitioner has sought a reference by invoking Section 2-
A of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act which was referred
by the Conciliation Officer and the following questions of
reference were framed by the Government Order No.1125-
30/Dehradun-CP25/68/2005 dated 15.02.2006 to the
following effect:-
 "D;k lsok;kstdksa }kjk Jfed Jh fouksn dqekj iq= Jh
jkeiky flag ifjpkyd dh lsaok; sa fnaukd 31-03-2004 ds vkns'k ls lekIr
fd;k tkuk mfpr rFkk vFkok oS/kkfud gS \ ;fn ugh arks lEcfU/kr Jfed
D;k fgrykHk vuqrks"k ikus dk vf/kdkjh gS ,ao vU; fdl fooj.k d s
lkFk\''"
13. The learned Labour Court by the impugned award
dated 6.2.2010 has denied the claim of the petitioner and
thereby has upheld the order of dismissal dated 31.3.2004
as well as the appellate order dated 3.1.2005, affirming the
order of dismissal, against which the present writ petition
has preferred by the petitioner on the following major
grounds which are being summarized as under:-
"(a). Because court erred in not considering the
services of the petitioner has been dismissed by
respondents on false and non existing grounds

-7-
(b). Because dismissal cannot be sustained as the
charges which were basis of the proceedings were
never proved against the petitioner.
(c). Because Labour Court has not discussed the
stand taken in the written statement and taken by
the petitioner in the proceedings before it and no
finding has been recorded.
(d). Because learned Labour Court, Dehradun
had also committed grave illegality in not
considering the vital aspect of the matter that it is
the admitted position of the case that the vehicle in
which the petitioner was plying the bus as
conductor was double crew and the duty of the
petitioner was only up till Rishikesh. All the
passengers seated in the bus were having the
tickets.
(e). It was hence proved on the fact of record
that the charges levelled against the petitioner
were false and concocted. It was levelled against
the petitioner by the inspecting squad merely to
make out a case and nothing more.
(f). All the aforesaid facts find no discussion in
the impugned award, whereas these were the
specific pleas of the petitioner that were never
dealt by any authority and merely considering the
case of the respondent authorities unilaterally, the
punishment as well as the impugned award has
been passed.
(g). Because learned representative of the
petitioner advanced his arguments pointing out all
the discrepancies/perversities in the enquiry report
and the termination but was not considered despite
being argued.
(h). Because the quantum of punishment but
learned Labour Court has not even cared to deal
with those arguments and went on to mention that
they were cursorily argued by the representative of
the petitioner. Thus the impugned award deserves
to be set-aside on that score alone."
14. In the grounds taken, agitated and argued by Mrs.
Neetu Singh, the counsel for the petitioner before this
Court is that the very foundation stone of the entire
proceeding which happens to be initiated on 19.11.2001 by

-8-
issuance of chargesheet, there had been material procedural
flaw. It is unequivocal proposition of law that once in a
departmental proceeding, when a statement of witness is
recorded, in that event, a cross examination of the witness
whose statement is recorded at the time of inspection
conducted on 25.10.2001, and reliance has been placed on
those statements, for holding a delinquent employee liable
for a misconduct under Rule 61 of 1980. It is mandatory
that the delinquent employee ought to be granted an
opportunity to cross examine the witness otherwise failing
which it will vitiate the proceedings and it would deprive
the delinquent employee on effective opportunity of
hearing.
15. The learned counsel for the petitioner has questioned
the validity of order of dismissal precisely from the view
point that the procedure adopted by the inquiry officer was
bad in the eyes of law, for the reason, the documents, on
which, the reliance was placed were not supplied to him
and also the witnesses whose statement were recorded and
relied were not examined and they were not permitted to be
cross-examined. The High Court of Delhi in the case of
Dr. Pushkar Saxena vs. Govt. of NCT of Delhi & others in
W.P.(C) No.7592 of 2001in its para 9 has held as under:-
"9. In Bidyug Chakraborty (Prof.) v. Delhi
University & Ors.: 2009 VI AD (Delhi) 1, on
complaints of sexual harassment being made
against the petitioner before this Court who was
working in University of Delhi, an Inquiry
Committee was set up to investigate the
complaints. The Committee submitted its report
holding the petitioner guilty of sexual harassment.
Pursuant to the report of the Committee, the

-9-
Executive Council of the Committee warned the
petitioner and also debarred him from holding any
administrative post in the University for a period
of 03 years. The petitioner filed the aforesaid writ
petition seeking quashing of the Memorandum,
whereby warning was given to him and he was
debarred from holding any administrative post in
the University for a period of 03 years as well as
the report of the Inquiry Committee. Ordinance
XV-D of Delhi University which applied to the
inquiry held against the petitioner inter alia
provided that the complainant and the accused
would be called separately so as to ensure freedom
of expression and an atmosphere free of
intimidation. The Committee did not give an
opportunity to the petitioner for verbal cross-examination of the witnesses examined by it and
copies of their statements were not supplied to
him. After completion of examination of the
witnesses no opportunity was given to the
petitioner to produce defence witnesses though at
the time of supplying the charge-sheet to him he
was given an opportunity to give names of the
witnesses whom he wanted the Committee to
examine. Allowing the writ petition a Division
Bench of this Court, inter alia, held as under:
"As noted earlier, no opportunity was given to the
petitioner for verbal cross examination of the
complainant. A perusal of the inquiry report shows
that the committee informed the petitioner that he
could cross examine the complainant by giving
written questions to the committee. In our
opinion, mere permission to give written
questions to the committee for cross examination
of the complainant does not fulfil the legal
requirement on the part of the Inquiring
Authority, to give opportunity to the delinquent to
cross examine her. Cross examination by giving
written questions to the inquiring authority can
never be as effective as verbal cross examination
and cannot be its proper substitute. While putting
questions to a witness the examiner does not
know what answer the witness would give to the
questions put to him/her. It is, therefore, not
possible for him to formulate the next question

-10-
without taking into consideration the answer
given by the witness. The answer given by the
witness to one question may lead to further
questions from the examiner on the same line, in
order to elicit truth from the witness and to
impeach his/her trustworthiness. Moreover,
asking the petitioner to give written questions for
cross examination was confined in respect of the
complainant alone. No opportunity was given to
the petitioner even to give written questions for
cross examination of other witnesses examined by
the committee. It was imperative on the part of the
Inquiring Authority to give opportunity to the
petitioner for her cross examination not only of
the complainant but also of the other witnesses
examined by it. Denial of opportunity to cross
examine the complainant and other witnesses
examined by the committee constitutes gross
violation of principles of natural justice. Rule
14(16) of CCS/ CCA rules mandates the
Disciplinary Authority to ask the delinquent to
state his defence which is to be recorded unless it
is a written statement. Clause 17 of this rule
requires the Inquiring Authority to then call upon
the delinquent to produce his evidence. He may, if
he chooses so, examine himself in his defence. In
the present case, though at the time of serving
charge sheet upon the petitioner, the committee
asked him to give list of witnesses whom he wanted
to be examined by the committee, no such
opportunity was given to him after the committee
had examined the complainant and other witnesses
in support of the complaint. The committee was
required not only to give an opportunity to the
petitioner to produce his witnesses but those
witnesses were to be cross examined by the
petitioner and not by the committee, though, it
would have been open to the committee to examine
them after they had been examined by the
petitioner and had also been subjected to cross
examination."
16. The service rules as applicable on the Corporation
employees, is that as were prevailing in the undivided State

-11-
of U.P. were called as U.P. State Transport Corporation
Service Rules, 1981, these rules which are applicable with
UTC do contemplate specific procedure under which the
proceedings for imposing the punishment by way of major
or minor penalty for the misconduct could be imposed and
dealt with. The penalty which constituted to be the major
penalty under the rules with which we are concerned in the
present case is provided under Sub Rule (7) of Rule 63 i.e.
dismissal. The procedure for imposition of major penalty
is provided under Sub Rule (3) of Rule 64. It provides that
a cross-examination of the witnesses is must, the Sub Rule
(3) of Rule 64 is quoted hereunder:-
"64. (i) Without prejudice to the right to terminate
the service in accordance with regulation 29 no
order (other than order based on facts which had
led to his conviction in a criminal court) of
dismissal, removal or reduction in a rank, which
includes, reduction to a lower post or time scale or
to a lower stage in the time scale but excludes the
reversion to a lower post of a person who is
officiating on a higher post, shall be passed against
an employee unless he has been afforded adequate
opportunity of defending himself.
 (ii) The ground on which it is proposed to take
action shall be reduced in the form of a deninite
charge or charges which along with the evidence
proposed to be relied upon in support of the charge
shall be communicated to the person charged and
he shall be required, with in a reasonable time, to
put in a written statement of his defence and to
state whether he desires to examine or cross-examine any witness and whether he desires to be
heard in person. He shall also be informed that, in
case he does not file a written statement of his
defence, it will be presumed that he none to furnish
and orders will be passed (ex-parte).
 (iii) If the employee desires or the Enquiry Officer
considers it necessary an oral inquiry shall be held
in respect of such allegations as are not admitted.

-12-
At the enquiry such oral evidence shall be heard as
the Enquiry Officer considers necessary. The
person charged shall be entitled to cross-examine
the witnesses, to give evidence in person and to
may for sufficient reasons to be recorded in writing
refused to call or examine any witness."
17. Even Regulation 84 of the Rules of 1981, which deals
with saving clause, deals with the Regulation in relation to
other matters, which had not been covered under the Rules
of 1981. Hence, in principle, the provisions of Uttarakhand
Government Servant (Disciplinary and Appeal) Rules of
2003, which would also be attracted to be too attracted,
which in its Rule 7(VII), while dealing with the procedure
for imposition of major penalty, under Rule 7(VII)
provides for an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses
to the delinquent employee under Rule VII of the
Disciplinary & Appeal Rules, 2003 is quoted hereunder:-
Procedure for imposing major penalties.
7. Before imposing any major penalty on a Government
Servant, an inquiry shall be held in the following manner:-
(i) The Disciplinary Authority may himself inquire into
the charges or appoint an Authority subordinate to him as
Inquiry Officer to inquire into the charges.
(ii) The facts constituting the misconduct on which it is
proposed to take action shall be reduced in the form of
definite charge or charges to be called charge sheet. The
charge-sheet shall be approved by the Disciplinary
Authority.
 Provided that where the Appointing Authority is
Governor, the chargesheet may be approved by the
Principal Secretary or the Secretary, as the case may be, of
the concerned department.

-13-
(iii) The charges framed shall be so precise and clear as to
give sufficient indication to the charged Government
Servant of the facts and circumstances against him. The
proposed documentary evidences and the name of
witnesses proposed to prove the same along with oral
evidences, if any, shall be mentioned in the chargesheet.
(iv) The chargesheet, along with the copy of documentary
evidences mentioned therein and list of witnesses and their
statements, if any shall be served on the charged
Government Servant personally or by registered post at the
address mentioned in the official records in case the
chargesheet could not be served in aforesaid manner, the
chargesheet shall be served by publication in a daily news
paper havingh wide circulation:
 Provided that where the documentary evidences is
voluminous, instead of furnishing its copy with
chargesheet, the charged Government Servant shall be
permitted to inspect the same before the Inquiry Officer.
(v) Where the charged Government Servant appears and
admits the charges, the Inquiry Officer shall submits his
report to the Disciplinary Authority on the basis of such
admission.
(vii) Whether the charged Government Servant denies the
charges the Inquiry Officer shall proceed to call the
witnesses proposed in the chargesheet and record their oral
evidence in presence of the charged Government Servant
who shall be given opportunity to cross-examine such
witnesses. After recording the aforesaid evidences, the
Inquiry Officer shall call and record the oral evidence

-14-
which the charged Government Servant desired in his
written statement to be produced.
18. What is revealed from a coordinated study of service
jurisprudence is that cross examination becomes a vital and
integral part of disciplinary proceedings because cross
examination often facilitates in extracting the truth from a
witness otherwise whose statement is to be relied for
against delinquent employees for establishing his guilt.
This Court is of an opinion failure to provide opportunity
to cross examination would mean depriving an effective
opportunity of hearing and would violate principles of
natural justice.
19. Even in the judgment it has been held by the Hon'ble
Apex Court in the case of Managing Director ECIL vs. B.
Karunakar as reported in AIR 1994 SC 1074, in its Para 4,
which reads hereunder:-
"4. It will be instructive to refer briefly to certain
authorities on this aspect of the matter. We may first
refer to the decision of this Court in Khem Chand v.
Union of India, 1958 SCR 1080: (AIR 1958 SC 300),
where two questions squarely fell for consideration,
viz., what is meant by the expression" reasonable
opportunity of showing cause against the action
proposed" and at what stage the notice against the
proposed punishment was to be served on the
delinquent employee. After referring to the decisions of
the Judicial Committee in R, Venkata Rao v. Secretary
of State for India (1937) 64 Ind. App.55: (AIR 1937 PC
31), and of the Federal Court in Secretary of State for
India v. I.M. Lall (1945) FCR 103:(AIR 1945 FC 47),
the Court held that the reasonable opportunity
envisaged by the provisions of Article 311(2) as
originally enacted, was at the following stages:

-15-
 (a) An opportunity to deny his guilt and
establish his innocence, which he can only do if he is
told what the charges levelled against him are and the
allegations on which such charges are based;
 (b) an opportunity to defend himself by cross-examining the witnesses produced against him and by
examining himself or any other witnesses in support
of his defence; and finally
 (c) an opportunity to make his representation
as to why the proposed punishment should not be
inflicted on him, which he can only do if the competent
authority, after the inquiry is over and after applying
his mind to the gravity or otherwise of the charges
proved against the government servant tentatively
proposes to inflict one of the three punishments and
communicates the same to the government
servant......."
The Court further held that the substance of the
protection provided by rules like Rule 55 of the Civil
Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules
promulgated on May 27, 1930 under Section 96-B of
the Government of India Act, 1915 (sic), was bodily
lifted out of the said Rules and together with an
additional opportunity embodied in Section 240(3) of
the GOI Act, was incorporated in Article 311(2) so as
to convert the protection into a constitutional
safeguard. The Court also held that the opportunity to
show cause against the penalty proposed should be
given after a stage has been reached where the charges
had been established and the competent authority had
applied its mind to the gravity or otherwise of the
proved charges tentatively and proposed a particular
punishment. It was necessary to state so, since in that
case no notice was served upon the appellant there
when the competent authority accepted the report of the
Inquiry Officer and confirmed the opinion that the
punishment of dismissal should be inflicted on him, and
no cause, therefore, could be shown by him. On the
other hand, by the first notice itself which
communicated the charges, the appellant was called
upon to show cause as to why he should not be
dismissed from service, although the notice further

-16-
called upon the appellant to state in reply whether he
wished to be heard in person and whether he would
produce his defence.
Still further question that was required to be
answered was whether when the disciplinary authority
issued notice to the employee to show cause against the
punishment, proposed, the employee had the right also
to represent that he was not guilty of the charge itself
and the findings recorded against him were wrong. This
question was squarely answered by this Court in Union
of India v. H.C. Goel: (1964) 4 SCR 718: (AIR 1964 SC
364). The Court pointed out there that it was well-settled that the public servant entitled to the protection
of Article 311 must get two opportunities to defend
himself. He must have a clear notice of the charge
which he is called upon to meet before the departmental
inquiry commences, and after he gets a notice and is
given the opportunity to offer his explanation, the
inquiry must be conducted according to the rules and
consistently with the requirements, of natural justice.
At the end of the inquiry, the Inquiry Officer
appreciates the evidence, records his conclusions and
submits his report to the Government concerned. That
is the first stage of the inquiry. After the report is
received by the Government, the Government is entitled
to consider the report and the evidence laid against the
delinquent public servant.
In General Manager, Eastern Railway v. Jawala
Prasad Singh (1970) 3 SCR 271:(AIR 1970 SC 1095), it
is reiterated that the duty of the Inquiry Officer ends
with the making of the report. The disciplinary
authority has to consider the record of the inquiry and
arrive at its own conclusion on each charge. Even if the
inquiry committee makes a report absolving the
employee of the charges against him, the disciplinary
authority may on considering the entire record come to
a different conclusion and impose a penalty. A
reference is made in this connection to H. C. Goel's
case (AIR 1964 SC 364) (supra)."
20. Learned counsel for the petitioner, Mrs. Neetu Singh,
while referring to the judgment, it has been held by

-17-
Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Khem Chand vs. Union
of India & others reported in AIR 1958 SC 300, while
dealing with the expression the reasonable opportunity of
showing cause against an action propose has been
considered the impact of para 19 of the said judgment and
has held that reasonable opportunity as envisaged under
Article 311 (2) would also include an opportunity of cross-examination.
"19. To summarise : the reasonable opportunity
envisaged by the provision under consideration
includes -
 (a) An opportunity to deny his guilt and establish
his innocence, which he can only do if he is told what
the charges levelled against him are and the
allegations on which such charges are based;
 (b) an opportunity to defend himself by cross-examining the witnesses produced against him and
by examining himself or any other witnesses in
support of his defence; and finally
 (c) an opportunity to make his representation as to
why the presupposed punishment should not be
inflicted on him, which he can only do if the
competent authority, after the enquiry is over and
after applying his mind to the gravity or otherwise of
the charges proved against the government servant
tentatively proposes to inflict one of the three
punishments and communicates the same to the
government servant.
In short the substance of the protection provided by
rules, like R. 55 referred to above, was bodily lifted
out of the rules and together with an additional
opportunity embodied in S. 240(3) of the
Government of India Act, 1935 so as to give a
statutory protection to the government servants and
has now been incorporated in Art. 311(2) so as to
convert the protection into a constitutional
safeguard."

-18-
21. In reply thereto, the learned counsel for the
Uttarakhand Transport Corporation, Mr. Ashish Joshi
vehemently submits that in accordance with the statement
of the Assistant Transport Inspector as recorded before the
inquiry officer, who was a member of the inspecting team.
The written statement was recorded of the passengers
which was duly endorsed by the delinquent employee. He
further submits that for the purposes of extending the
arguments and to reply the arguments of petitioner's
counsel to the effect that no opportunity to cross-examination was provided to the petitioner. He argues that
it is mandatory for the delinquent employee to argue and to
show as to what prejudice is caused to him due to non
providing of an opportunity to cross examine. Meaning
thereby in principle he admits that no opportunity of cross
examination was provided to the petitioner, which is
contrary to the service rules of 1981, which mandates cross
examination as to be one of the steps to be resorted for
imposition of major penalty.
22. This argument as extended by the learned counsel for
the respondent is too far fetched and premature. The
reason being that the prejudice cause could only be
assessed when actual opportunity to cross-examination is
provided because in the process of cross-examination, an
employee who is charged with certain allegations of
misconduct get an opportunity to solicit answers or to pose
question in a manner to retrieve the truth in the absence of
providing an opportunity to cross examination, meaning
thereby, the employee was deprived to have an opportunity

-19-
to retrieve the truth of the allegations, from the cross
examine of the witnesses whose statement was relied by
the inquiry officer.
23. Meaning thereby the inquiry as conducted against the
petitioner in relation to the charge leveled against him on
9.11.2001, suffered from a procedural flaw, as there was no
complete adherence of principle of natural justice as
contemplated under Rule 311(2) of the Constitution of
India as laid down in the judgment as reported in AIR 1958
SC 300 (supra). Hence on this count itself, the order of
dismissal dated 31.3.2004 is faulted off. When the
decision making process adopted for the action impugned
is faulty itself then the entire conclusion and reasoning too
is rendered to be defective. In such a situation, the
principle as laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court that in
service matters when a delinquent employee is facing a
charge which is based upon the statement of a witness, he
is mandatorily to be provided with an opportunity of cross
examination of the witnesses. On this limited count itself,
the order impugned deserves to be quashed because this
aspect has not been taken into consideration either by the
appellate authority or by the learned Labour Court while
rendering the award dated 26.12.2010.
24. At this stage, the learned counsel for the respondent-Corporation submits that if there is a flaw or any right of
the petitioner has been prejudiced due to non providing of
due and adequate opportunity of cross examination, in that
eventuality the matter deserves to be relegated back to the

-20-
inquiry stage, so that, the flaw which has occurred in
adopting the procedure may be specified. This argument
yet again will amount to be an admission by counsel, that
cross examination of witnesses was must, which has not
been provided to the petitioner.
25. Apparently, this argument seems to be quite
appealing, but I am of the considered opinion that if an
employee has been made to suffer by facing the wrath of
procedure and an order of dismissal was passed due to
inaction on part of the employer by adopting faulty
procedure having civil consequence due to action taken, he
should not be placed back at the place from where the
proceedings have been initiated so as to surmount his
apathy cumulatively, which were faced by them as a
consequence of order of dismissal passed at the behest of
the employer in non compliance with the procedure and
principles of natural justice, the employee is entitled to get
the benefit for that.

26. This writ petition succeeds and is accordingly
allowed. Impugned award dated 06.12.2010, the appellate
order dated 3.1.2005 and order of dismissal dated
31.3.2004 are set aside. The respondents are directed to
reinstate the petitioner with 50% back wages only.
27. No order as to costs.
 (Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.)
